  12.3

KISS ANCLES
In the previous section, First Contact, we showed how three angles could be used to show the main elements of the
kiss, instead of shooting from three angles, you can swing the camera round the actors, to cover the same angles.
As you can see from this example, this works best if the camera is slightly above the actors, looking down at them.
This approach also makes it possible for one character to dominate the scene, rather than having it be a shared
moment. Here, Liv Tyler s character is the subject of the scene, so the camera passes behind the male actor. It s her
face that we see most clearly at all points through the kiss.
'

'

Most people, when they kiss, lean to the right. In film, however, we need a little more variety, and in a shot like this, it
helps if the actor who is facing camera changes the angles of her head as the camera moves. At the beginning of the
shot she is leaning towards the camera, and by the time the camera has swung around behind the other actor, her
head has angled towards the camera again. This isn't always essential, but is important if you want the scene to be
more about her than about them as a couple.

You can also see how she has angled her body away from the other actor. This may be because it makes for a more
beautiful framing, or because of the character's reluctance to kiss, but it is the sort of detail you need to be aware of.
Most kissing scenes are shot poorly, and it's worth trying to be better than average, because a good kissing scene is
enough to make some people go back to see a film again (or buy the DVD).

GETTING DOWN
If your kissing scene is to progress to a more sexual one, then at some point you need to get the characters to lie
down. This can be quite awkward to film, but there are a few elegant solutions. One of the more beautiful solutions is
to cut from the kiss to a shot of an empty bed, and then have the characters fall back into the shot.
One of the beauties of this technique is that it eliminates a potentially awkward moment where the actors stop
kissing and begin to move toward the bed; if you want this to feel like a flowing sex scene, rather than an awkward
one, the cut to empty space can solve your problem.
At this point you may want your characters to talk more, to kiss more or to undress each other, and this set-up has
the advantage of being suitable for all three.

There are a few pitfalls to avoid. Be careful not to have the lower character go down too fast, or there can be a
trampoline effect which looks comical. It's also best if they come into shot almost as one; if one falls back, and then
the other falls in later, the result can again be comical. It should look as though they have simply flowed out of a kiss
and into this position.
This works best when the characters are not actually in an embrace, so you can put a lit le space between them,
before the intimacy is resumed.

OUT OF BODY
Some of the finest sex scenes ever shot show almost nothing of the bodies, but concentrate on the actors' faces. You
can even shoot such scenes where the actors are almost completely clothed (so long as this makes sense story-wise).
For this to work you require exceptional actors, but you may find that any actor will enjoy the challenge of a sex scene
that is largely about the work they do with their faces and their feelings, rather than how much skin we get to see.

Set up your cameras so that both actors' faces are in shot. As you can see from these examples, the actors should
not be facing each other directly, but have their faces close. There are many ways to achieve this, and a thousand
variations, but essentially you are trying to get both faces in shot as much as possible, while making it plausible that
they are exploring each other's bodies (and eventually making love).
The camera can either be at their head height, or slightly above, and it's best to begin this with a fairly tight framing.
You can move further out as the scene progresses, to reveal more of their movement, and more of their bodies if
required but keep their faces angled toward the camera, so that the focus remains on their expressions. It's how they
,

see each other, rather than what we see of them, that matters most.

FACING UP
One of the great challenges with intimate scenes, as has been expressed many times, is trying to keep both actors'
faces in view at once. In this example, the effect is achieved by careful positioning of the actors within the frame.
The woman is lying back, and although she is in conversation with the man (as they engage in foreplay), her head is
thrown back to some extent. She's turned it more towards the camera than towards him. He continues to simulate
'

making eye contact with her, even though he probably can t see her eyes.

The man is also lying off to one side of her slightly, because if he was laying directly on top her of, her body would
be obscured and his head would be at the wrong angle. Although this shot looks easy and comfortable, it is actually
quite precisely staged and may be quite difficult for the actors. It does, however, enable you to achieve a beautiful
framing, without being a gratuitous body-shot. It works best for scenes where the characters are still talking, rather
than just having sex.

MOMENTS OF CONNECTION
When the talking is over, and the scene is more about body contact and eroticism, it takes skill to reveal the right
details without looking forced. In this example the camera captures just a glimpse of Ziyi Zhang's face, as she throws
her head back. Then we see her ribs, and the man's hands on her body.

This type of set-up is highly erotic as it takes the focus away from the faces and directly to the body. It is also worth
noting that this is probably far more erotic than if she was naked, because of the expectation it brings; expectation
and suggestion are more erotic than pure obsen/ation of a naked body.
The follow-up shot moves to an unusual angle, looking back down at the two of them, so that her face is upside
down In the frame. In fact, her face takes up only a small part of the frame, and the mingled bodies fill the
rest. Because the two of them appear to be upside down, this captures the dizzying sensation of an electrifying
sexual encounter.

A WORLD OF DETAILS
When directors shoot sex scenes they often want to achieve a sense of great eroticism, but without a hint of
pornography. One way to achieve this is to attempt to capture the sensation of actually having sex; rather than
observing two people, why not put the camera right in there with them so we feel we re part of the experience. That
way we feel the movement and scuffle of clothes and bodies, and catch glimpses of the tiny details of clothing and
flesh, just as we do in the real world.
'

This one brief shot, from Stealing Beauty, shows nothing more than a blurred hand, shadow and a hint of bra. A long
lens has been used, to throw everything out of focus but the bra. This brief moment is one of many glimpses that
make us feel the proximity of this sex scene. Although we also cut back to see the two lovers kissing and touching
each other, it is these glimpsed moments that draw us into their experience and make it one of the most sexually
charged scenes on film.

 CONCLUSION
When you direct a film, you have a lot on your mind. The hours are long, sleep is short and the pressure is high. And
yet, in the midst of the circus, you are required to be as creative as you have ever been. As well as getting a strong
performance from your actors, you need to shoot in a distinctive way that reflects your story. This is no easy task.
Writing this book helped me realize that the more intimately I knew technique, the easier it was to create under
pressure. Time is always running out on a film set. After months or years of thinking about a film, you often have just
moments to make a new choice or solve a problem. And then you live with that decision forever. To people who ve
never worked in film, it seems implausible that we can spend 12 hours getting two minutes of usable footage. For
those who work in the industry, it seems like a miracle if we get that much. I hope this book will help you develop a
way of seeing shots, and thinking up your own, that will make you able to work creatively when time is running out.
'

The better you know your craft, the easier it is to create. I've often heard filmmakers say they don't care about
technique, or the history of film, and they just like to "be creative." Sometimes that works. But usually, you see
filmmakers on set just "getting the coverage" because there was a technical problem and they couldn't think of
a new solution in time. If they had a bit more knowledge about technique, they could probably have created
something better.
This lack of vision is often hidden behind shaky camera work and fast edits. But if you want to deliberately create
a film to communicate a story, you need more control than that. This doesn t mean you have to plan every shot in
advance, but when technique becomes second nature, it s easier to be original. Think of Yoda in The Empire Strikes
Back, telling Luke to unlearn what he has learned. When you know something well enough to "unlearn" it, you are
'

'

on the path to greatness. Unfortunately, many people think the short cut is to avoid learning the technique in the first
place. History shows they are wrong. The better educated you are about all aspects of filmmaking, the better you will
be at making films.

Now that you know 100 Master Shots, you are better equipped than most filmmakers. Your task is to adapt them,
improve on them, and build your own arsenal of workable shots.
CONCLUSION

225

 I was inspired to write this book because I saw that there are filmmakers out there who refuse to be average, and
'

who find new ways to create. For them, it s not about popcorn and grosses, but about making a great film. The
challenge you face is to avoid being average. It takes a lot of time and effort to direct anything, but by the time you

get on set, the pressure to get the job done without mistakes turns many a potential genius into a coward. 1 hope
these techniques inspire you to be courageous in your filmmaking. Whatever the pressure no matter how tired you
are, choose greatness.
,

THE ASPECT RATIO of a movie, meaning the ratio between
the width and height of the screen, plays a defining role in
how the rules of composition are applied when organizing
visual elements in a shot. Since the early stages of cinema,
filmmakers experimented with a variety of frame shapes,
prompted by aesthetic considerations, technological innovation, as well as economic pressures; studios eventually
settled on a squarish shape in the early 1930s, which remained unchanged until the introduction of widescreen aspect ratios in 1952. A handful of aspect ratio options became
standardized soon after, with most films using one of two
major widescreen formats ever since. The shift from celluloid film to digital video reignited the exploration of the aspect ratio as a more active tool for the creation of cinematic
images, because it lets filmmakers easily generate virtually
any frame shape they want during postproduction. As a result, aspect ratios that had gone unused for decades are
making a comeback, and heretofore unseen ratios that offer
completely new ways to implement the rules of composition
are being used to make movies with inventive, unique visual
approaches. Figure 1 shows the most popular aspect ratios
prevalent after the shift to digital filmmaking, demonstrating
how each screen shape alters the amount of visual information included in the frame. The widest ratio used in modern
filmmaking is 2.39:1 (originally 2.35:1 until the 1970s), called
"anamorphic" or "scope" (a); this ratio is often associated
with big-budget blockbusters ever since its introduction in
the early 1950s, when studios were desperate to attract audiences back into movie theaters with lavish productions that
featured exotic locations and top tier talent. The wide scope
of this ratio showcases locations and landscapes more than
characters, due to the extra room that is inevitably included

at the sides with most shot sizes, like in this medium closeup of Hugh Glass (Leonardo DiCaprio), a frontiersman left
for dead in Alejandro G. Iñárritu's historical survival drama
The Revenant. Another extremely common widescreen aspect ratio is 1.85:1, also called “flat” (b). The slightly narrower width can present characters and locations equally
well, and closely approximates the aspect ratio of HDTVs,
1.78:1 (also expressed as 16:9)(c). Bridging the gap between
the extra wide 2.39:1 and the taller 1.85:1 aspect ratios is an
increasingly popular screen shape originally developed by
legendary cinematographer Vittorio Storaro, called "Univisium"; at 2:1, it can accommodate wide landscapes as well
as characters without too much extra space at the sides of
the frame, and almost completely fills the screens of HDTVs
and smartphones (d). Although the advent of widescreen aspect ratios all but eliminated what had been the standard
since 1932, called the "Academy ratio" of 1.37:1 (e), it has
been resurrected in a number of high profile films recently,
particularly in period-piece narratives that seek to evoke the
genre aesthetics of early films. The squarish shape of the
Academy ratio favors the presentation of characters over
locations, which can barely be included in the frame when
shooting tighter shots like medium close-ups and close-ups.

technique allows 2.39:1 or 1.85:1 films to be released in
their original aspect ratio in movie theaters and in 1.78:1 for
HDTV broadcasting without the need to include black bars
to fill the empty portions of the screen. All of these aspect
ratios offer different compositional options, and also raise

FRAME AXES define the two-dimensional space used for the
composition of your shots. They comprise a horizontal, or xaxis, a vertical, or y-axis, and a third axis that denotes the
perceived depth of the frame, the z-axis. Filmmakers commonly employ a variety of techniques to overcome the inherent flatness of the frame by emphasizing the z-axis, creating
the illusion that space extends into the frame itself. One of
these techniques can be seen in Quentin Tarantino's Once
Upon a Time... In Hollywood (figure 3), where Cliff Booth
(Brad Pitt), a colorful Hollywood stuntman, is framed against
a number of characters using the relative size depth cue
technique (examined later in this chapter). Perceived distances and movement along each one of these axes can also
be manipulated by the type of lens used, camera movement,
and lighting, among other means, to alter the visual relationship between subjects and the space around them.

frame into thirds along its width and height, "sweet spots"
are created at the crossing points; placing important visual
elements over these spots is a common technique to create aesthetically pleasing compositions. The horizontal lines

and extreme long shots, and the vertical lines can guide the

Thirds, however, is for the creation of shot compositions that
feature proper amounts of "looking room" and "headroom"
when framing human subjects. In relatively tighter shots,
like medium close-ups, for instance, subjects are placed
over a vertical line depending on which side of the frame
they are facing: the left if they are looking towards the right,
or the right if they are looking left. This framing ensures
that they are given an empty space designed to balance the
composition by countering the visual weight of a subject’s
gaze, or "looking room". When looking room is added ignoring the Rule of Thirds (for instance, by placing a subject
at the center of the frame, or at the opposite side entirely,
giving them no looking room at all), a composition can feel
"static" and visually tense, which filmmakers sometimes exploit to suggest something unusual, abnormal, or dangerous is happening in a scene. The subject's eyes in a medium
close-up are usually lined up along the top horizontal line,
ensuring "headroom", or the spacing between a subject’s
head and the top of the frame, is properly sized. The amount
of headroom that should be included varies depending on
shot size; the general rule is that the wider the shot, the
larger it should be, and vice versa. In a medium close-up,
for instance, the top of the head should be cropped to give
a subject the right amount of headroom (despite the misnomer in this case), while in a medium shot it should not reach

the top of the frame. This is why the Rule of Thirds should
not be applied mechanically, but rather organically, depending not just on the shot size, but also on other aspects of the

the headroom and looking room should be placed. Figure

HITCHCOCK'S RULE is an amazingly simple yet extremely
effective compositional principle to guide the framing of a
shot. The rule was derived from a series of groundbreaking
interviews Alfred Hitchcock gave François Truffaut that were
eventually collected in Truffaut's book Hitchcock/Truffaut.
In their talks, Hitchcock made several references to how he
varied the size of a subject in the frame according to their
emotional importance to prompt audience engagement.
This concept eventually became known as Hitchcock's Rule,
which states that the size of a subject in the frame should
be directly proportional to its importance in the story at that
moment. The more important someone or something is, the
larger the area of the frame they should occupy. This principle can be applied whether you have only one or several
visual elements in the frame, and whether or not the reason behind the visual emphasis is known to the audience at
the time. Figure 5 shows Hitchcock's Rule in action during a
scene from Martin Scorsese's Taxi Driver, when Travis Bickle
(Robert De Niro), a depressed Vietnam War veteran on a path
of self-destruction, purchases black market handguns from
an underground dealer (Steven Prince), signaling a point of
no return for his character. The significance of the handguns
and their purchase is underlined by letting them occupy the
entire bottom half of the frame, while Travis and the dealer
are cropped, slightly out of focus, and relegated to the background of the composition.

BALANCED AND UNBALANCED COMPOSITIONS can make
powerful visual statements about the subtext of a scene. You
can create a purposely balanced or unbalanced composition
by taking into account that every visual element in a frame
carries with it a visual weight, and their relative size, color,
brightness, and placement can affect how they are perceived
by an audience. This concept makes it possible to compose
images that "feel" balanced when their visual weight is evenly
distributed, or unbalanced when it is concentrated in only one
area of the frame. Although the terms balanced and unbalanced have no inherent value judgement in terms of cinematic
composition, it is not uncommon to find balanced compositions being used to convey order, uniformity, and predetermination, among other ideas. Unbalanced compositions, on the
other hand, are often relied on to communicate a sense of
uneasiness, turmoil, and tension. Despite these typical associations, the kind of ideas that can be suggested by balanced and unbalanced compositions ultimately depend on
the context in which they are used; a balanced composition
can suggest "chaos" if it is properly contextualized. Figure 6
shows conventional implementations of both types of compositions, from John Hillcoat’s Australian western The Proposition. In (a), a balanced composition where almost every visual
element was arranged symmetrically in the frame instills a
sense of peacefulness and order during a Christmas dinner

FOCAL LENGTH refers to the measurement from the optical
center of a lens (the point where the image is flipped and
reversed) to a camera's sensor in millimeters. This distance
is one of the main ways we classify lenses, and can always be
found engraved on a lens. The three main types of lenses in
terms of focal length are called "normal", "wide-angle", and
"telephoto". Focal length is a determinant factor in the way
perspective looks, how much of a scene can be seen, how
fast or slow movement is perceived, and the look of facial
features, among other visual characteristics. It also has a
proportional relationship with a subject's degree of magnification in the frame; for instance, if you want to reduce the
size of a subject in a shot by half, you can simply switch to a
lens with half the focal length you are using (if you're shooting with a 100mm lens, you would have to switch to a 50mm
lens), and vice versa. While this might seem a very simple
way to “dial in” the size of a subject in the frame, it is important to remember that you will also be changing what can be
seen around and behind the subject in the process, because
by changing your focal length you will also be changing the
angle of view.

ANGLE OF VIEW measures the extent of a scene a lens can
encompass across the x, y, or diagonal axes, expressed in
degrees. Angles of view are directly related to focal length;
shorter focal lengths produce wider angles of view, and longer focal lengths result in narrower angles of view. A lens'
angle of view provides a fundamental way for filmmakers to
control what is included in a shot. For instance, you could select a short focal length to expand the angle of view when you
want to include more of the environment in a shot, and when
visual elements need to be excluded, you could switch to a
longer focal length with a narrower angle of view.
FIELD OF VIEW, or the measurement across the x, y, or diagonal axes a lens can cover at a given distance expressed in degrees, has the same relationship with focal length as a lens'
angle of view: shorter focal lengths have wider fields of view
and longer focal lengths have narrower fields of view. Field
of view is not, however, exactly analogous to angle of view.
A lens' angle of view is fixed and cannot be changed, but the

is a function of both the angle of view and the camera’s placement in relation to a subject. If a camera is brought closer

extreme close-up
The extreme close-up concentrates the audience’s attention
on a tiny portion of a character or on small objects, making
it ideal for isolating minute, single visual details from the rest
of a scene. Using an extreme close-up instantly generates
the expectation that what is being shown is important to the
narrative (a classic application of Hitchcock’s Rule), which
is often exploited to instill a sense of anticipation in the audience. A common strategy, for instance, involves isolating a
seemingly unimportant detail that ends up playing a critical
role later in the story. In this case, the first instance of the
extreme close-up prompts the audience to expect its subject to be significant in some way, so that, when they see it
again and its narrative purpose is revealed, it does not seem
unjustified and artificially convenient. Extreme close-ups can
also function to conceal a character's identity or the full extent of an object by withholding key visual information from
an audience, generating a sense of mystery and tension. Their
limited view of a subject, however, makes them less than ideal
to showcase emotion or nuances of behavior through a character's facial expressions or body language, except in general, almost symbolic terms. When extreme close-ups feature
an extremely small detail of an object or a character they are
called "macro shots" (covered on page 153), and are obtained
with specialized lenses that allow getting much closer to a
subject than conventional lenses. At such close distances,
they can showcase more fundamental visual characteristics, like textures, colors, or patterns to the point of abstraction, but, narratively, they still function as extreme close-ups.
When used this way, their visual content might not be directly
related to the narrative, but nonetheless adds to the overall
dramatic tone or thematic context because of the abstract
qualities or associated meanings it can suggest.

In the example on the opposite page, from director Julio
Medem’s Spanish drama Sex and Lucía, an extreme closeup focuses the audience’s attention on the path of a single
tear as it rolls down the cheek of Elena (Najwa Nimri), a
woman who was earlier shown having a casual sexual encounter with a man while swimming in the ocean under a
full moon. The sequence opens with a graphic match that
dissolves from a shot of the moon to an extreme close-up
of a pregnancy test showing a positive result; upon learning the news of her unexpected pregnancy, Elena sheds a
tear that slowly makes its way down her cheek until it falls
on the test, partially smearing it. The visual emphasis the
extreme close-up places on the tear (because of its extreme magnification and the way the camera tilts down to
follow its path across her face) implies it is a key element of
this sequence, but also prevents identifying the precise emotion that caused it. If a conventional close-up had been used
instead of an extreme close-up, for instance, Elena's facial
expression and the reaction it communicated would have
been the main narrative point of this moment; by excluding them, the audience can consider alternate meanings
for the extreme visual emphasis placed on the tear. When
the narrative context and highly stylized presentation of the
shots immediately preceding it are taken into account, the
connection between the tear's salt water and the ocean in
which her fateful encounter took place is easy to make, and,
by extension, also with other associated meanings, like tide
cycles, moon cycles, and menstrual cycles, all of which are
connected to the revelation of her pregnancy. The choice of
an extreme close-up to showcase the tear makes it possible to suggest that it represents all of these things to Elena,
adding a symbolic and even poetic context to this scene.

technical considerations
Depending on the size of the subject and the level of magnification required, telephotos, wide-angles, and macro lenses
can all be used to shoot an extreme close-up. Zoom lenses
are at a disadvantage if they are used as wide-angles, however, because a zoom lens set at a short focal length has a
longer minimum focusing distance than an equivalent prime,
which can potentially prevent you from capturing very small
details. The native lenses used in smartphones make it relatively easy to shoot extreme close-ups, because their shorter
focal lengths (around 4mm, equivalent to roughly 33mm in
the 35mm format) result in them having very short minimum
focusing distances (commonly less than 4 inches). In cases
where the subject is too small to be captured with conventional lenses, a specialized lens, called a macro, offers an
alternative, since it is specifically designed to let you get extremely close to a subject (although there are other ways to
get similar results, examined on page 156).
At such short focusing distances, however, it can be
very difficult to keep a subject in focus because of how shallow the depth of field becomes; virtually any movement in
front of or behind the camera can shift the plane of focus
to an unwanted area along the z-axis of the frame. Using
smaller apertures can make things easier, provided extra
light can be added to compensate for the reduction in exposure. Special care also needs to be taken when shooting subjects with a lot of repetitive, fine detail (a common problem
when shooting fabrics, for instance), which can result in the
appearance of very distracting rainbow-like distortions that
shift across areas of the image, known as a "moiré effect".
Closing down the aperture can significantly reduce and even
eliminate these artifacts, but it can also compromise image
quality because it can prevent shooting with a lens' "sweet
spot" (the aperture setting that produces maximum sharpness). Another option is to slightly adjust the distance to the
subject, provided footage can be previewed at full resolution
(with an external field monitor set to 1:1 pixel mapping, for

instance) to confirm the moiré has been eradicated. Whether
the subject is a detail of a person or a tiny object, lighting
should be planned and executed as carefully and thoughtfully as if you were shooting a key close-up of an actor. When
you are on set it can be easy to forget that although your subject might look tiny and even unimportant in person, it will
look gigantic and imposing when it is seen on a large screen.
The magnification in an extreme close-up not only makes a
strong visual statement about its subject, but also magnifies
any errors or inconsistencies in framing, lighting, or focusing
it may have, so it is especially important to be as technically
exacting as possible when taking these shots.
Although in some cases the tightness of the framing can preclude the inclusion of all of the lights that were
used in wider shots within the same scene, the overall
lighting continuity should be maintained to a certain degree
(meaning that you should not suddenly light an extreme
close-up using a low-key, film noirish look if the shot right
before had high-key, shadowless lighting, and vice versa).
Generally speaking, however, the greater the difference in
shot size between the shot immediately preceding or following an extreme close-up, the more license you will have
to add, move, or change the intensity of the lighting between shots without being too distracting or obvious. This is
especially true if the wider shots also happen to include a
lot of visual elements and/or movement in the frame, which
will make it even more difficult for an audience to notice
visual discrepancies. For instance, the extreme close-up on
the opposite page, from director Spike Lee's crime drama
Clockers, is followed by a long shot with lighting that shows
a lot more of the interrogation room where the scene takes
place. If that same lighting setup had been used for the
extreme close-up, however, the detective's reflection on the
eye would not have been as easy to spot as it is, and the key
moment of the story it communicates would not have been
as visually striking.

close-up
The close-up is a relative newcomer to the cinematic vocabulary; before the visual language of movies was developed to include the large variety of shots we have today, early
silent films told stories almost exclusively with wide shots,
replicating the experience of watching a stage play. The introduction of the close-up as a narrative tool would have a
tremendous impact not only in the way audiences connected
with characters, but also in the development of a more naturalistic style of acting that departed from the exaggeration
commonly seen in the theatre. What sets the close-up apart
from all other shots is its ability to give the audience intimate
access to nuances of a character’s behavior and emotion (especially those that play across the face) that cannot be fully
appreciated in wider or even tighter shots. A close-up does
not simply showcase emotion, but the specific and unique
ways a character experiences it. The physical closeness and
intimacy of a close-up can elicit a strong emotional connection with a subject, making an audience care, empathize,
love, and even hate a character. Filmmakers routinely enhance this connection by using visual conventions designed
to minimize the impact of anything that can distract from
a performance; for instance, backgrounds in a close-up are
usually kept out of focus to help visually isolate a subject,
and normal or slight telephoto focal lengths are typically
preferred over wide-angle lenses to avoid distorting an actor's facial features in distracting or unnatural ways. These
conventions have been so widely adopted that it is rare (although not impossible) to find a close-up of a character
that features a deep depth of field, or one taken with a lens
that overtly distorts facial features, like a fisheye lens. The
close-up's ability to motivate emotional involvement with a
character requires that it be used sparingly, or else its im-

pact can become narratively meaningless within a film's image system through overuse. For this reason, close-ups are
commonly reserved for moments when a character makes
an important decision, delivers an especially meaningful line
of dialogue, or reacts to a particularly important piece of information (the "turning points" of a story).
Director Andrew Stanton’s WALL·E, the story of a
charming little robot in charge of collecting garbage hundreds of years after humans were forced to leave a contaminated Earth, features a classic use of a close-up during
a key moment of its story. The last of his kind, WALL·E distracts himself by keeping a collection of random artifacts he
finds during his work shifts, like spoons, lighters, and toys.
One day, he stumbles upon a tiny plant, unbeknownst to
him an incredibly significant event, since we later learn its
existence means Earth has become habitable again. This
moment of discovery is punctuated by a textbook example of
a close-up (opposite page), which, although completely computer generated, features every visual convention commonly
found in them, from a shallow depth of field that blurs the
background to focus our attention on the plant's reflection
in WALL·E's "eyes", to his placement in the frame following
the Rule of Thirds to give him the proper amount of headroom
and looking room. These visual cues, along with the strategic
use of a close-up for this particular moment, unmistakably
signal to the audience they're watching a key event, even
though they are not yet aware of its actual significance. Interestingly, although WALL·E lacks facial features, showing
him in a close-up in this narrative context also prompts us
to read an emotion on his "face", because of the storytelling expectations this shot size generates. When used in this
manner, a close-up can achieve its full narrative potential.

a wide-angle lens to show more of a scene behind a character can also distort facial features

technical considerations
Using normal or slight telephoto lenses is the norm when
shooting close-ups, although sometimes wide-angle lenses
or longer telephotos are also used to purposely distort a
character's facial features; most often, however, distortion is
avoided because it can distract from an actor's performance.
Setting lenses to wider apertures to blur backgrounds is also
common, especially when using shorter focal lengths (since
their effect on z-axis perspective can make shallow depths
of field harder to notice). When shooting indoors with artificial lighting, compensating for using a wide aperture simply
involves cutting light with dimmers, scrims, nets, or by moving lighting instruments farther away from subjects. When
shooting outdoors in daylight, using neutral density filtration, either fitted on a matte box or through your camera if it
has it, is the easiest way to cut enough light to make it possible to have a shallow depth of field. Although technically you
could also lower your sensor's sensitivity to compensate for
the extra light a wide aperture lets through, deviating greatly
from your camera's native ISO should be avoided whenever
possible since it can potentially introduce an unacceptable
amount of video noise.
A camera's sensor size can also indirectly impact
your ability to produce a shallow depth of field, but this is
due to variables related to image magnification and focusing distance and not the sensor size itself. Smartphones, for
instance, make it difficult and in some situations practically
impossible to have blurry backgrounds; conversely, cameras
with full frame sensors can blur backgrounds excessively,
requiring smaller apertures to keep relevant visual details
sharp enough. While having visual elements behind a subject out of focus is expected, it is important to consider that
every degree of blurriness you use in your images will communicate a meaning about your character or your story. For
instance, you may want a background to be blurry enough to
keep your audience's attention centered on a subject, but not
so blurry they cannot tell where a scene is taking place.

While showcasing details on an actor's face is the main aim
of a close-up, capturing too much of it can sometimes be
counterproductive. Depending on a subject's skin texture,
turning your camera's sharpness and detail settings too high
can result in less than optimal results, which can be particularly evident in a close-up (for instance, when make up cannot
conceal an actor's less-than-perfect complexion, or when it
is less than expertly applied and becomes glaringly apparent). Additionally, your lens can also exacerbate the appearance of sharpness, because some optical designs enhance
contrast and resolution more than others. Because of this,
professional cinematographers almost always shoot tests
to assess, among other things, not just how a particular lens
interacts with their camera's image processing, but also to
ascertain what sharpness and detail settings will work best.
In most cases, the lighting of a close-up will showcase nuances of behavior on an actor's face; for this reason, lights are usually aimed from a direction that reveals,
and not conceals, the visual impact of facial expressions.
Another common practice involves ensuring eyes have
bright reflections on them to prevent a "dead gaze", which
can make a character look unnatural and lifeless. These eye
reflections can also be instrumental in visualizing a character's emotions, feelings, or other psychological states, by
controlling their size, shape, location, and number. Although
they are often produced by lighting that is already present,
they might also require adding special lights (called "eye
lights") or large reflectors close to the camera so they can
be seen, and actors may also need to be blocked to ensure
their eyes catch these reflections. When adding eye lights,
it is important they do not drastically alter the look of your
lighting; while close-ups allow you to tweak your setup (especially when preceded or followed by shots that are sufficiently different in angle or size), lighting changes should not
be so apparent that they break continuity and distract from
the narrative point of a scene.

medium close-up
Medium close-up shots include a character roughly from
the shoulders to almost the top of the head; this shot is
tighter than a medium shot, but slightly wider than a closeup (as with all shots that use the human body for reference,
the cutoff points between them are not strictly defined).
Like the close-up, the medium close-up showcases facial
expressions, letting audiences catch small nuances of behavior and emotion; however, the slightly wider framing
also lets body language reveal hints about their demeanor
by the inclusion of the shoulders in the frame. This shot
size also incorporates some of the immediate area behind a
character, letting you suggest dramatic, symbolic, or expository connections between them by selectively including or
excluding visual elements. For this reason, although the primary function of a medium close-up is to elicit an emotional
connection with a character, you should not ignore what is
seen around your subject, how it is lit, or how sharp or blurry
it looks. You could, for instance, adjust your camera's height
so that a particularly meaningful set detail, texture, or color
(perhaps as part of the image system you created for your
movie) is clearly visible in the background. When used strategically with long shots, medium shots, and close-ups, medium close-ups can also play an essential role in modulating
the dramatic intensity of a scene. A typical implementation
of this principle can be seen whenever an exchange between
characters is covered with wider shots, like long shots or
medium shots, until someone discloses an important piece
of information, at which point a medium close-up is used to
showcase a character’s reaction; this sudden visual emphasis signals to the audience that the revelation is especially
significant, and increases their emotional involvement with
the character at that moment.

Jean-Pierre Jeunet’s romantic comedy Amélie, the story of
a Parisian girl (Audrey Tautou) who one day decides to dedicate herself to improving the lives of neighbors and strangers alike, routinely uses medium close-ups during moments
when she selects someone to receive a random act of kindness, and when she discovers something particularly meaningful about their personal lives (the latter often shown with
instances of her breaking the "fourth wall" to address the
audience directly), among others. In the example on the
opposite page, Amélie has just learned a young man she
has a crush on is just as quirky and eccentric as her (he
likes to collect photographs of footprints on wet cement,
keeps recordings of funny laughs, and works at a carnival’s haunted house dressed as a skeleton). The medium
close-up used during this moment perfectly showcases
her reaction to this news: her devilish smile and coy body
language reveal she can hardly contain her happiness, and
a slight high angle (commonly used to indicate a character feels physically or psychologically vulnerable) suggests
she feels self-conscious after being unable to conceal her
emotions. Her awkwardness is also visualized by a central placement in the frame that purposely subverts the
looking room convention, indicating something unusual is
taking place. These choices are complemented with a shallow depth of field that blurs the background and focuses
our attention on her facial expression and body language,
while a wide-angle lens makes her head, and especially her
sparkly eyes, look larger than normal. The resulting look is
carefully designed to make us empathize and relate to her,
making the many moments like this one that appear in the
film one of the reasons audiences became so enchanted
with Amélie.

Subject placement does not follow the Rule of

technical considerations
Normal and slight telephoto lenses are commonly used
when shooting medium close-ups, because they do not add
any noticeable distortion to a character's facial features.
However, sometimes wide-angles and longer telephotos are
used to give a character a somewhat stylized, or slightly unnatural, or even completely distorted look. Lens choice can
also be guided by the need to manipulate the perception
of motion within the frame. Depending on the direction of
movement and the effect that needs to be achieved, a medium close-up could be taken with a telephoto lens (for instance, when trying to make a character moving along the
z-axis look like they are covering less ground than they really
are) or with an extreme wide-angle lens (to accelerate their
motion under the same circumstances).
Another factor that can determine your choice of focal length is the amount of visual information that needs to
be seen behind a character. Since a medium close-up can potentially include a sizable portion of the surrounding area (as
seen in the example from Perfume in this chapter), your lens
choice might depend on the angle of view needed to include
however much or little of the background needs to be seen.
It is important to note that after a shot is framed, you cannot
simply switch lenses to see more or less behind a character
without also changing the camera's position to compensate
for the magnification or demagnification of the image the
new focal length provides. If you frame a medium close-up
with a normal lens, switching to a telephoto to exclude more
of the background will require you to move the camera farther
away from the subject to keep their size constant. While this
might not present a problem when shooting outdoors, since
you will likely have enough room to reposition the camera, it
might not be something you can do when shooting indoors in
a confined location. You may also choose a particular focal
length to control how far or how close something behind a
character appears to be, by using wide-angle lenses to extend distances along the z-axis (the technique used in the

example from Perfume on the previous page), or telephotos
to compress them (as shown in the example from Léon: The
Professional on page 66). One aspect that should not be considered when selecting a focal length is how shallow or deep
you want the depth of field to be, because when subject size
and aperture setting remain constant, changes in focal length
have no effect on it.
When shooting outdoors on a sunny day, there are
several techniques to light a medium close-up (and most
character shots) depending on the time of day. For instance,
when the sun is high in the sky, it is common to use a butterfly (a large, collapsible aluminum frame fitted with diffusion
material) over actors to change the quality of sunlight from
hard to soft; this is done to reduce unflatteringly hard shadows across faces, particularly under the eyes. This technique,
however, results in a difference in light quality between a
subject and the background, but most audiences will not
register anything is amiss, especially when using a shallow
depth of field to keep background detail out of focus. When
the sun is lower in the horizon, subjects are usually blocked
so that sunlight functions as a backlight, and a key light is
added (usually a large, powerful HMI light diffused with a butterfly), often while also bouncing light from the opposite side
to add texture across their faces. Although medium closeups include more visual information than close-ups, their
primary function is still to showcase a character's emotions.
For this reason, all of the lighting conventions we associate
with close-ups (like adding eye glints, tweaking the lighting
established in previous shots, and giving subjects a more
visually compelling look) are equally applicable to medium
close-ups. However, since backgrounds occupy more space
in these shots, they also require special attention to communicate a narrative point. For instance, lighting could be used
to highlight a meaningful object, or to reveal a texture that
adds a certain mood, or a color could be added to contribute
a symbolic meaning, among others.

medium shot
Medium shots include one or more characters from the waist
up along with a sizable portion of their surrounding area.
They are tighter than a medium long shot, but wider than a
medium close-up, which provides just enough room in the
frame to showcase a character's body language while still
being close enough to underline nuances of behavior and
emotion through facial expressions. The wider perspective of
medium shots also allows a character's costume to provide
expository information about their personality, social status,
and other character traits. When they include more than one
subject, they can also help visualize relationship dynamics
through character placement and blocking, for instance, by
placing them far apart to imply there is a conflict between
them, or by putting them closer together to suggest they are
compatible or in agreement. This is one of the reasons why
medium shots are often used for two shots, group shots, and
OTS shots. While a character is the main subject of a medium
shot, they are not visually isolated from their surroundings
(like they are in close-ups, for instance), making it possible
to create meaningful narrative connections between them.
A common practice involves framing characters so that a
meaningful aspect of a location is visible behind them in a
way that comments, informs, or reveals details about their
personality, emotional state, or attitude. Medium shots are
also very useful as transitional shots between wider, more
visually expository shots, and tighter, more intimate shots,
allowing you to gradually increase or decrease audience involvement within a scene. For instance, a conversation between two or more characters could be covered with medium
shots until someone says something particularly important
or meaningful; at this point, a medium close-up or a close-up
can be inserted, adding dramatic weight to this moment. Af-

ter this beat, the rest of the conversation could return to using
medium or wider shots. The added emphasis provided by the
tighter framing of the close-up or medium close-up works
because wider, expository shots, like medium shots, are used
initially to establish facts of the locale, characters, and spatial
relationships before a change in the dramatic direction of the
scene is introduced. Of course you could also cut directly from
long shots to close-ups, bypassing medium shots and a build
up of tension altogether; in this case, the drastic change in
shot sizes could be interpreted by the audience as an equally
drastic change in the dramatic direction of the scene.
Director Wes Anderson’s signature style is well known
for its elaborate and imaginative art direction, quirky costume
designs, and oddball characters; unsurprisingly, medium
shots that showcase these elements are used extensively in
most of his films. A typical example can be seen on the opposite page, from his comedy The Royal Tenenbaums, the story
of three siblings who have a troubled relationship with their
eccentric but lovable father. In this scene, Margot Tenenbaum
(Gwyneth Paltrow), an adopted member of the family, hides
from her husband to smoke a cigarette; the relatively wide
area covered by the medium shot, coupled with thoughtful
lighting, depth of field, body language, and costume choices,
allows audiences to make strong visual connections between
her and the various items in the background (the darkroom
paraphernalia, the animal motifs on the wallpaper, the pink
telephone) that communicate a lot of expository information
about her character. The shot's frontal, symmetrical composition (another one of Anderson's visual trademarks) also
helps present the visually dense composition efficiently, almost like a catalog of parts, allowing the audience to quickly
identify every item in the frame.

technical considerations
Medium shots showcase a character and a sizable portion
of a location, allowing audiences to make visual connections between them; your lens choice can greatly enhance
or diminish the way they are presented by manipulating the
perceived relative distances between subjects. For instance,
you might want to make a key aspect of a location behind
a character look as if it is farther away than it really is; in
this case, you could use a wide-angle lens, since it can
make distances along the z-axis appear to be longer than
they really are. You could also achieve the opposite effect, and make it look as if something in the background
is much closer to a character, by using a telephoto lens to
compress, rather than expand, distances along the z-axis.
While medium shots can be obtained with virtually any focal length, the amount of space available in a location can
sometimes force you to use one type of lens over another.
For instance, if a medium shot is taken in a cramped indoor location, like a tiny apartment or a bathroom, you
may not have enough room to use a long telephoto lens to
compress perspective while still framing your subject from
the waist up, as this shot size requires. Instead, you would
have to use a normal or even a wide-angle lens, since their
much wider angle of view needs a significantly shorter camera to subject distance to frame a medium shot.
Your lens choice can also affect the appearance of
visual relationships between subjects through your depth of
field, by using selective focus to make particular visual elements easier or harder to discern by an audience. This approach, however, requires having control over the brightness
levels of your lighting to compensate for exposure changes as
you open up or close down the aperture. You may also adjust
your camera's ISO instead (switching to a higher ISO when
closing down or to a lower ISO when opening up), but keep in
mind that, depending on your camera's dynamic range and
image processing technology, deviating significantly from its
native ISO can introduce unacceptable levels of video noise.

For this reason, it is preferable to compensate for changes
in aperture setting through adjustments in lighting intensity,
and not by changing your sensor's sensitivity.
Lighting can also play a significant role in the way
visual connections between a subject and a location are perceived. A common strategy involves controlling the lighting
ratio (the relationship in brightness levels between a subject and the background/foreground) by lighting each plane
of depth in a composition separately. This allows making
the main subject brighter, darker, or just as bright as the
background, depending on the narrative point that needs to
be communicated. Most often, characters are kept slightly
brighter than everything else in a composition to prompt
audiences to focus on their performance; the difference in
brightness used in these cases can range anywhere from
slightly less than a full f-stop of light to complete underexposure (when a background is practically black). For instance,
note the difference in brightness levels between characters
and backgrounds in the medium shot from Wes Anderson's
The Royal Tenenbaums, at the beginning of this chapter, and
the medium shot from Chantal Akerman's Jeanne Dielman,
23, Quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles on the opposite
page. In Anderson's The Royal Tenenbaums, Margot stands
out ever so slightly from the background thanks to a subtle
spotlight effect, evidenced by the darker edges of the frame.
The slight difference in brightness is designed to focus our
attention on her, but not to the point we will disregard the
various props and overall art direction around her, since they
provide key information about her character. In Akerman's
Jeanne Dielman, Jeanne is lit in a more naturalistic style,
and far from standing out in the composition, she seems
to blend with the background, which in some areas is actually brighter than she is. Although not greatly dissimilar,
the lighting approaches used in these medium shots suggest
dramatically different types of relationships between the
main subjects and the locations they occupy.

medium long shot
Medium long shots show a single or multiple characters from
approximately the knees up; they are wider than medium
shots, but tighter than long shots. According to film history
lore, medium long shots first appeared in American Westerns, and were created out of a necessity to include a cowboy's gun holster in a fairly tight shot, which cannot be done
using a conventional medium shot (this explains why they
are also known as plans américains, or “American shots”, in
French). Medium long shots pull away from intimate proximity and only provide a general sense of a character's mood
or emotion through their facial expressions; however, they
showcase body language and their surrounding area simultaneously, making them ideal for situations when a narrative connection between these elements needs to take
precedence. When they include multiple subjects, they can
also visualize relationship dynamics (by their relative placement within the composition, through the implementation
of Hitchcock’s Rule, and with balanced/unbalanced framings, among other techniques); their wider perspective also
makes them ideal for group shots and emblematic shots.
Like long shots and medium shots, medium long shots are
also used in combination with tighter shots to modulate the
audience's emotional involvement; a common implementation of this principle entails placing them after particularly
intense moments to reconfigure previously established dynamics between characters. Since medium long shots can
be visually dense, they are often kept on-screen longer than
tighter shots with fewer details, which gives audiences more
time to scan their compositions. For this reason, it is especially important to always check the frame one last time
right before shooting to ensure they do not contain any unwanted visual elements.

The medium long shot on the opposite page, from Luc Besson’s Léon: The Professional, features a small exchange between the titular character (Jean Reno), an expert hitman,
and Mathilda (Natalie Portman), a precocious 12-year-old
girl he saved from a gang of corrupt cops. In a previous
scene, Mathilda proved her intent to become a killer for
hire by blindly shooting a gun out of an apartment’s window, forcing Léon to make a decision about her future. The
medium long shot that follows functions as a reveal; Léon
appears first in the frame as he walks towards us, tricking
the audience into thinking he has ditched Mathilda. As the
shot continues, Mathilda enters the frame revealing that he
has in fact decided to let her tag along. The narrow angle
of view of a long telephoto lens, coupled with a low camera
placement, allowed the filmmakers to exclude everything
from the frame except for Léon, Mathilda, and the buildings
in the distance. A shallow depth of field further concentrates
our attention on the pair by isolating them from their surroundings, letting us focus on every detail of their outfits,
the strange assortment of props they are carrying, and the
demeanors communicated by their body language. The exclusion of extraneous visual elements is especially critical in
this example, because the entire scene plays out within this
single medium long shot, giving audiences ample time to
analyze the dynamics of their relationship as well as the dramatic differences in height and overall physical appearance
between them. If this shot had been taken with a wide-angle
lens, or with a deeper depth of field, or if the camera had
been placed slightly higher, the passersby and heavy traffic
likely present in the busy Manhattan street location would
have prevented the jarring visual juxtaposition of these characters from being the sole focus of this composition.

technical considerations
Since medium long shots showcase a character’s body language and a significant portion of their surrounding area,
your choice of focal length can be instrumental to let you
control what gets included in the frame. In the example from
Léon: The Professional, for instance, the narrow angle of view
of a long telephoto lens allowed the exclusion of all the traffic, sidewalks, and bustling crowds one would expect to see
in the busy Manhattan street where the scene takes place,
letting the audience focus their attention solely on the overall
appearance and body language of the characters during their
exchange. A different approach was used in the example from
1984, where a much shorter focal length made it possible to
include critical visual details (the poster of "Big Brother", the
screen playing Winston's confession, the emptiness of the
bar) within the same composition to establish the multiple
visual and thematic relationships the filmmakers wanted to
communicate in this scene. When trying to include or exclude
visual elements, it is important to consider that longer focal
lengths can dramatically change what is seen in the background of a shot with minimal adjustments in camera position (but require longer distances from the main subject),
while shorter focal lengths require significant changes in
camera placement to do the same (but can be much closer
to a subject). This means that your ability to control the visual content of a frame at a given location through your focal
length will depend on the distance needed to frame a particular shot size and how much space is available along the
z-axis between the camera and your subject.
One tip to help you quickly assess how a given lens
will render your scene in a location is to understand the relationship between subject size, focal length, and focusing distance; this principle can be particularly helpful in situations
where you need to frame a character at a certain shot size,
like a long shot or a medium close up, but you also need to
include or exclude visual elements from their surrounding
area to make a narrative point. For instance, if you frame a

subject with a 50mm lens but then decide there are things
in the background that should not be seen, you could switch
to a 100mm lens, which will double the size of your subject,
and then move the camera back so it is at twice the distance
it was before to render it back to its original size. The difference would be that now only half of what was visible in the
background would be included in the composition, because a
100mm lens has a much narrower angle of view than a 50mm
lens. If you wanted to include visual elements instead, you
would do the opposite: switch to a 25mm lens and bring the
camera closer to match the same subject size you had before, only now you will see twice as much of the background
as you did previously.
Medium long and wider shots taken indoors generally require large, powerful lights to illuminate the more
spacious areas included in the frame. For instance, in the
example from 1984, the light sources used to simulate sunlight streaming through the front windows of the cafe had to
be strong enough to reach all the way to the back wall for the
poster of "Big Brother" to be seen clearly. Shooting a medium
long shot outdoors on a sunny day presents a different issue;
the wide area this shot covers means it will be more difficult
to control the quality of light with a butterfly over your actors
(the technique used in the medium close-up from Perfume:
The Story of a Murderer, on page 56). Although shooting night
exteriors with only available light is feasible thanks to advancements in CMOS sensor technology, using a very high
ISO to compensate for low-light conditions might not always
be desirable; depending on your camera's sensor, a high ISO
may introduce a level of video noise that may render your images unusable. For this reason, obtaining the best possible
image quality still requires supplementing or completely replacing available light when shooting wide shots at night outdoors, with all the logistic requirements this entails (powerful
lights, extra tall stands or cranes, and the generators needed
to power them, among others).

long shot
The long shot includes one or multiple characters from
head to toe in the frame, along with a significant portion of
the environment. The perspective of this shot is too distant
to showcase emotional cues on a character's face, although
their general demeanor can still be gleaned by their body
language and actions. Alternatively, the long shot's inability
to showcase specific emotions can be exploited to add tension and mystery to a scene; for instance, by using it instead
of a medium close-up or a close-up to purposely conceal
a character's reaction or identity at a key moment. Unlike
tighter shots, long shots highlight a location as much as or
even more than a character, allowing it to contribute a meaningful narrative context to a moment or an action; their wider
scope also permits establishing more explicit visual connections between them. Long shots are commonly framed from
a lower camera height, since this allows excluding a sizable
portion of the ground in front of a character and leaves more
room in the frame to showcase a location's key visual characteristics. Like extreme long shots, long shots are often
used as establishing shots (covered on page 93), and are
typically placed right before an interior scene to identify the
setting where subsequent action is supposed to take place.
Long shots are also sometimes shown at the culmination
of a scene, usually featuring a composition that visualizes
a character's emotional or psychological reaction to a particularly meaningful event. When used strategically in conjunction with tighter shots, long shots can help to gradually
increase or decrease an audience's emotional involvement
during key moments of a scene. For instance, an exchange
between characters could be covered with long shots and
medium shots until something critically important is said,
at which point a medium close-up is used; after this beat,

cutting to a long shot that visualizes the revelation's dramatic aftermath (by using Hitchcock's Rule, or an unbalanced
composition, for instance), can bring the scene's dramatic
intensity down, letting audiences assess the impact of what
just transpired.
Alex Cox’s biopic Sid and Nancy, a film that charts
the mutually destructive relationship between Sex Pistols
bassist Sid Vicious (Gary Oldman) and an American groupie,
Nancy Spungen (Chloe Webb), features several long shots
that visually connect them with much of the drugs, alcohol,
violence, and emotional strife that permeated their world.
In the visually stunning image on the opposite page, a long
shot perfectly captures the unorthodox nature of their romance, showing them as they share a loving kiss in the
midst of a filthy back alley while garbage rains down in slow
motion from above. The composition's low-angle and highly compressed perspective (obtained with a long telephoto
lens) allowed the filmmakers to place the couple against a
bright gap between the buildings in the background, making them stand out in the composition even though they are
only semi-silhouetted (subverting the lighting convention of
keeping a shot's main subject brighter than anything else in
a composition). The telephoto's flattening effect also made
the blurry buildings in the distance easier to notice, enhancing the effect of the shallow depth of field to further focus
the audience's attention on the area of the frame where they
are kissing, and visually merged them with the refuse raining
down on them, underscoring the idea that they are considered castoffs and trashy by society. Every visual aspect of this
long shot is designed to present this moment as a romantic
and even beautiful chapter of their relationship, despite the
unconventional (yet strangely fitting) setting.

technical considerations
One of the ways the long shot visualizes relationships between a character and a location is by manipulating the
actual or apparent distances between them in the frame.
Since focal length can distort the appearance of perspective, it can be instrumental in effecting how these relationships are presented. A wide-angle lens, for instance, can
expand perspective along the z-axis, making backgrounds
appear more distant than they really are, which can visualize a strained emotional or psychological connection between a character and their surrounding area. Conversely,
a long telephoto lens can flatten perspective, making backgrounds appear unrealistically close to a character in the
foreground, which can imply a strong connection between
them. It is important to remember, however, that your ability to manipulate the appearance of perspective will be limited by the amount of space to set up a shot at a given location when using long focal lengths. If a long shot is taken
indoors with a long telephoto lens, for instance, there might
not be enough space to place the camera far enough to
counteract the magnification of the image while including a
character from head to toe in the frame. There are, however, other factors that can also influence visual connections
between a character and a location; lighting, exposure, art
direction, and camera or subject movement, among others, can (separately or in combination) enhance or diminish
them. Compressing perspective to make a background appear closer to a character will be harder to see if the lighting does not showcase this effect; likewise, if a background
happens to be a textureless, empty wall, even an extreme
compression effect can go unnoticed. Your focal length
choice should therefore complement, and not work against
or ignore, every other technical and aesthetic aspect of your
shot in addition to its composition. Selective focus can also
help manipulate visual relationships between characters
and locations; a shallow depth of field, for instance, can
blur a background to make details in it difficult to notice

while enhancing other aspects, like its color, or any shapes
produced by the blurriness. In these cases, the connection
with a character takes a more abstract or even symbolic
approach that can communicate a more complex emotional
or psychological idea to an audience.
Control over the depth of field will require being
able to adjust the lighting to compensate when opening
up or closing down the aperture, although changing the
ISO is also an alternative (but, depending on your camera, it
can have an adverse effect on image quality). When shooting outdoors in full sunlight, you will need neutral density
filtration to cut enough light when using a wide aperture
to blur backgrounds; on the other hand, when shooting
indoors with artificial light and a deep depth of field is
required, be prepared to have enough lights to compensate
for the smaller apertures needed to achieve it. Another
strategy to control how a background is perceived involves
the manipulation of distances along the z-axis with your focal length. Although you can shoot a long shot with any
lens, a long telephoto's magnification will make the background seem much closer than it really is because of its
flattening effect, which will make the blurriness produced
by a shallow depth of field a lot more noticeable than if the
same shot were taken with a wide-angle lens (which will
make the same blurry background appear to be farther
away). This is the technique that was used in the example
from Alex Cox's Sid and Nancy at the beginning of this
chapter to make the blurry buildings in the background more
prominent. The opposite effect can be seen in the example
from Michael Radford's 1984 (covered on page 68), where a
lens with a shorter focal length was used; its wider angle of
view required a shorter camera to subject distance to frame
the subject (in this case in a medium long shot), which in
turn made the background appear more distant, making it
difficult to notice everything in it is actually slightly out of
focus.

extreme long shot
Extreme long shots show a broad view of a location with one
or multiple characters seen from a distance that occupy a
very small area of the frame. The main subject of these shots
is the setting where the action takes place, since characters
are too distant for their facial expressions or body language
to reveal their demeanor in detail. The composition of extreme long shots is often designed to underline differences
in scale between a character and a location, establishing
spatial relationships between them and in the process emotional or psychological connections as well (by following or
subverting the Rule of Thirds, using balanced or unbalanced
framings, or by creating meaningful juxtapositions implementing Hitchcock’s Rule, among others). Depending on the
visual complexity of the location, the distant perspective of
an extreme long shot can sometimes make it difficult to spot
a character in the frame, making it particularly important to
ensure they are easy to notice if that is your intention. This
can be accomplished in a number of ways: for example, by
placing them in a relatively empty area of the frame, by using lighting to make them stand out, or by ensuring nothing
else in the composition is moving except them, to name a
few. High angles are commonly used in extreme long shots
when a location features wide, empty spaces, because they
show more of the ground around a character than eye-level
angles, and can better highlight how small they are in the
frame while making the location look particularly expansive.
However, if a location includes a tall structure of some kind,
like a building or a mountain, a high angle would not be as effective as shooting at eye-level to highlight differences in size
and scale between a subject and their environment. When
extreme long shots do not include characters and showcase
only a location, they are referred to as establishing shots (ex-

amined on page 93), although in some cases they can also
become extreme long shots; for instance, by first showing
just a location and then having a character enter the frame.
An iconic example of an extreme long shot can be
seen on the opposite page, from Alain Resnais’ enigmatic
drama Last Year at Marienbad, the story of a couple who
meet at a luxurious hotel and discover that they may have
met previously and perhaps contemplated having an affair. The shost, one of many fascinating visual puzzles in
the film, features a symmetric composition that underlines
the geometric patterns of a vast, opulent garden; the overt
symmetry and balance of the composition is disturbed by a
number of people standing perfectly still on a central path
(evoking the statues around them). Strangely, they cast hard,
identical-looking shadows on what is obviously an overcast
day (at an angle that breaks the order established by the
rest of the visual elements in the frame), adding a surrealistic touch to the already oneiric tone of the film. Although
all of these compositional choices strongly imply a special
connection between the people and the garden, its meaning
is never addressed. Are the characters meant to be seen
as game pieces waiting to be moved, and the garden as a
giant gameboard, perhaps as an allegory of determinism?
Could they unknowingly be trapped in some kind of symbolic
purgatory? Philosophical interpretations aside, this image
demonstrates that beyond showcasing differences in scale,
the extreme long shot is also capable of expressing complex
ideas; only an extreme long shot could have simultaneously
included all the visual elements (a vast view of the garden,
multiple characters, an overcast sky) necessary to create
one of the most baffling and memorable images in the
history of cinema.

technical considerations
Since one of the aims of extreme long shots is to showcase
a location's scale, they are usually taken with wide-angle
lenses, because they can include more visual information
across the x- and the y-axis of the frame than normal or
telephoto lenses. Wide-angle lenses also tend to exaggerate distances along the z-axis, making locations with strong
leading lines (like buildings and highways), as well as those
with numerous relative-size depth cues (like street lights,
or people) look like they extend far into the horizon. While
extreme long shots can also be taken with telephoto lenses
when compressing, rather than expanding, distances along
the z-axis is needed, their narrow angle of view makes it
difficult to showcase the full breadth of a large location,
and they require significantly longer distances from a subject than wide-angle lenses to counteract their magnification.
Camera height can greatly enhance scale discrepancies in an extreme long shot; for instance, vast empty
spaces benefit from using higher camera positions, because
they can show a much larger area around a character while
simultaneously reducing the amount of space they take up
in the frame, making them look smaller than if the same
shot were taken at ground level. Getting the camera height
necessary for a high-angle extreme long shot used to require finding a location with an existing high vantage point
overlooking the area where the action would take place, rigging a platform with the necessary height, or renting a large
telescopic crane; thankfully, consumer drone technology
has greatly simplified getting extreme long shots from almost any height in virtually any location. Keep in mind, however, that flying a drone to get usable footage requires extensive rehearsals, favorable weather conditions (especially
in terms of wind speeds), and securing the certifications,
licensing, permits, or registrations that are required at your
particular location (more information on drone cinematography can be found in the aerial shot chapter on page 212).

Extreme long shots taken in full daylight rarely require artificial lighting, because natural light (even in overcast days)
is sufficient in most situations. However, they necessitate
extensive planning in case weather does not cooperate. Additionally, if the extreme long shot requires capturing light
at a particular time of day, logistics can become even more
complicated, but the results can be visually stunning. For
instance, Zhang Yimou’s acclaimed period drama Raise the
Red Lantern features an emblematic shot taken a few minutes before sunset that takes full advantage of the unique
quality of light at this time to add beauty and symbolism to
a key moment of the story (examined on page 142). Fortunately, there are plenty of smartphone apps that can predict
the sun's position at every minute of the day for any time of
the year, letting you previsualize the direction and length of
shadows for virtually any location. Additionally, with the help
of services like Google Maps' Street View feature and Google
Images, it is possible to conduct virtual location scouts to
get a good idea of what each place can offer before you actually visit them, saving you a lot of time and money while
also letting you work out your shoot's logistics much more
easily. Shooting extreme long shots outdoors at night using
only available light (even just moonlight), is actually feasible
thanks to advancements in CMOS sensor technology; however, while some cameras can be set to ISOs into the thousands (and even hundreds of thousands), not all of them can
yield a usable image due to the video noise very high ISO
settings produce. Also, just because there might be enough
available light to get potentially acceptable images, it might
not illuminate your location in a way that fits your extreme
long shot's narrative point. For this reason, shooting night
exteriors can still require having strong movie light sources
(and the generators needed to power them), as well as extra
tall light stands, cherry pickers, cranes, or other equipment
to elevate them at the height necessary to cover the large
areas in an extreme long shot.
